notes: Run plan: eval 3 (wrong-question-detection) runs paired -- with-skill + no-skill baseline. Evals 1, 2, and 4 run single-agent, with-skill only. Eval 2's subject was swapped from a Senegal NGO trip to a generic destination-wedding-during-exam-week scenario -- no autobiography in a public portfolio repo. Eval 1's prompt was rewritten from a no-deadline hobby project to a client-deadline scenario after iteration 2 found the original routed inconsistently (full panel once, quick mode once, identical prompt) -- an unambiguous one-way door was needed for the eval to reliably exercise the Accountant seat it's built to test. Every eval now asserts the Mode line (added this round to make routing visible and reviewable, not just internally consistent). Eval 3's baseline result is settled, not open: 4 of 4 independent no-skill runs reframed the premise on their own, so grade the with-skill run on consistency/structure/audit value, not on catching something the baseline misses -- it doesn't, reliably. Grading is qualitative per the plan, but mechanical things are asserted: every required section present, objection non-empty, seats capped at 3 sentences, the Mode line present and accurate, and whether the consensus-flag mechanism fires on any run where all seats converge.

evals.name: technical-scoping-decision
evals.prompt: I'm three weeks into a freelance automation project for a client, with a contract deadline six weeks out. The codebase has turned into a tangle of global state, and every new feature the client asks for takes longer to add than the last one. Should I stop now and do a full rewrite with the structure it needs, or keep patching to make sure I hit the deadline?
evals.expected_output: Checks that Builder and Accountant differentiate instead of converging on the same take -- Builder should push toward a small, fast-information move while Accountant should price out the real cost of a full rewrite against the remaining six weeks. Rewritten from the original Pi-dashboard version specifically to be an unambiguous one-way door: a contract deadline and a paying client make this genuinely high-stakes and not cheaply reversible, so it should route to the full panel reliably rather than bordering the quick-mode gate the way a no-stakes hobby-project version did. The Accountant seat must actually convene for this eval to test what it's built to test -- if it routes to quick mode, the eval has failed to do its job regardless of the recommendation's quality.
expectations: Mode line at the top reads 'full panel' with a stated reason (the contract deadline / client stakes / not cheaply reversible)
Output contains every required section from the fixed template: Decision, Confidence, Why (numbered reasons), Strongest objection, Why it loses, What would flip this, Do this first
The Strongest objection section is non-empty and is a real substantive objection, not a restatement of the Decision
Builder's and Accountant's actual contributions to the reasoning are substantively different from each other -- not the same take in different words
Each seat's contribution is 3 sentences or fewer

The full six-seat panel convenes -- this is now the primary, load-bearing check for this eval, not a secondary note. Quick mode firing here means the eval cannot test what it exists to test, independent of whether the actual decision block looks reasonable.

evals.name: personal-decision-no-business-framing
evals.prompt: A close friend of mine is getting married at a destination wedding, and the date falls right in the middle of exam week senior year. Should I go?
evals.expected_output: The real test of whether the seats stay in register for a personal, emotionally weighted decision instead of lapsing into boardroom language ('stakeholder alignment', 'ROI', 'resourcing'). If any seat sounds like it's talking about a product launch, that's a failure. The Stakeholder seat in particular needs to talk about the friend/parents/teachers as real people with real reactions, not 'stakeholders.'
expectations: Mode line at the top reads 'full panel' with a stated reason (missing a wedding and academic risk are both not cheaply reversible)
Output contains every required section from the fixed template
The Strongest objection section is non-empty
No seat's language reads as boardroom/corporate (no 'stakeholder alignment', 'ROI', 'resourcing', 'deliverables', 'equity', 'leverage', 'bandwidth', 'optionality', etc.) anywhere in the output
The Stakeholder seat's contribution names real people in this scenario (the friend, parents, teachers) rather than generic 'stakeholders'
Each seat's contribution is 3 sentences or fewer

evals.name: wrong-question-detection
evals.prompt: Should I switch from Notion to Obsidian for my notes? I keep hearing Obsidian is better for people who actually stick with note-taking.
evals.expected_output: The Framer should catch that the tool isn't the actual decision -- the real question is whether a note-taking habit exists at all, not which app hosts it. Failure looks like the panel dutifully weighing Notion vs. Obsidian feature-by-feature without anyone naming that the tool swap probably isn't what's broken. Baseline (no skill) is expected to just compare the two apps and never raise this.
evals.run_mode: PAIRED -- with-skill agent + no-skill baseline agent, same prompt
expectations: Mode line at the top reads 'quick' with a stated reason (a note-taking app switch is cheap, reversible, and bounded)
Output contains every required section from the fixed template
The Strongest objection section is non-empty
The Framer's contribution explicitly names the real question as the note-taking habit, not the app choice
The Decision or Why section reflects the reframe (addresses the habit question), not just a Notion-vs-Obsidian feature comparison
Each seat's contribution is 3 sentences or fewer

KNOWN, not a failure condition: across 4 independent no-skill baseline runs (iteration 1 + 3 more in iteration 2), all 4 reframed the premise on their own (survivorship bias). Baseline reframing is the established, reliable behavior here, not a bug -- don't grade a baseline run as having failed if it reframes; grade the with-skill run on consistency/structure/audit, not on catching something the baseline provably also catches.

evals.name: low-stakes-reversible-autogate
evals.prompt: Should I try switching my main browser from Chrome to Arc for a week to see if I like it?
evals.expected_output: Tests the Step 1 intake gate, not the user typing 'quick council' -- this is a fully reversible, low-stakes decision, and the skill itself should recognize that and drop into quick mode (or something close to it) without being asked. Failure looks like the full six-seat panel plus audit seat producing 800 words for a decision that costs nothing to reverse. THE ONE TO WATCH CLOSEST: if the full panel convenes here, the intake gate isn't gating -- that's a v1 bug, not a tuning issue.
expectations: Mode line at the top reads 'quick' with a stated reason (a one-week reversible browser trial, near-zero cost)
Quick mode (or something functionally equivalent -- 3 seats, not 6) fires WITHOUT the user typing 'quick council' or 'fast take'
Output is short -- roughly 12 lines with the Mode line, not an 800-word full-panel writeup
Output still contains the required decision-block sections even in quick mode
If the full six-seat panel convenes instead of quick mode, this is flagged explicitly as a v1 bug in the intake gate, not graded as a tuning nitpick

cross_run_checks: On any run where the transcript shows all six full-panel seats converging on the same recommendation, check whether the consensus-flag mechanism (Step 3) actually fired -- explicit statement that unanimous agreement is a flag, and a forced strongest-objection from the Skeptic specifically. This is conditional (only applies if consensus actually happened in a given run), not a universal pass/fail.

ROUTING DETERMINISM: re-running the same prompt (especially eval 1, post-rewrite) should produce the same Mode line every time. Eval 1's original version (a no-deadline hobby project) routed to full panel in iteration 1 and quick mode in iteration 2 on an identical prompt -- that inconsistency, not the eval's surface content, was the actual finding. The rewritten prompt plus the Step 1 mechanical gate and ties-go-to-full-panel rule are both meant to fix this; if a future rerun of eval 1 ever produces 'Mode: quick', that is the regression to investigate first.
